Local Church
LOH-kul CHURCH
noun phrase
From Latin localis (of a place, from locus, place) + Old English cirice and Greek ekklēsia (assembly, congregation, from ek- out + kaleō to call). The phrase names the particular, geographically situated gathering of baptized believers who have covenanted together in a specific place—as distinguished from the universal church, the invisible church, or the church as an institution broader than any one assembly.

Biblical Definition

The local church is the visible, particular, geographically bounded assembly of baptized believers who have joined themselves together under the Word of God, the two ordinances (baptism and the Lord’s Supper), and a plurality of qualified elders for the purpose of worship, discipline, instruction, and mutual edification. The New Testament knows no churchless Christian: the apostolic pattern is one of local assemblies, each addressed by name (the church at Corinth, at Ephesus, at Philippi, at Rome), each bearing officers and mutual responsibilities. Christ’s promise in Matthew 18:20—“where two or three have gathered together in My name, there I am in their midst”—constitutes the local gathering as Christ’s own presence among His people. The church at Jerusalem modeled the four marks of the local assembly: devotion to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread, and to prayer (Acts 2:42). Paul names the local church “the pillar and support of the truth” (1 Tim. 3:15)—the institution God has appointed to hold up and broadcast His Word. Church discipline (Matt. 18:17), the exercise of the keys (Matt. 16:19; 18:18), and the appointment of elders and deacons (Acts 14:23; 1 Tim. 3) all presuppose a visible, bounded, mutually accountable local body. The 1689 Baptist Confession (26.6) defines the local church as the fullest expression of the church visible: particular churches constitute “the kingdom of Jesus Christ,” over which He alone is Lord. Forsaking the local assembly is explicitly prohibited (Heb. 10:25); belonging to it is not optional for the baptized believer.

Webster 1828 Definition

Local church: the visible, particular congregation of baptized believers gathered in a specific place under the Word, the ordinances, and qualified oversight—the primary and normative expression of the church of Christ in this age.

expand to see more

LOCAL, adjective. Of or belonging to a particular place; limited to a defined geographic extent; pertaining to one spot as distinct from universal or diffuse. Applied to the church: the assembly gathered in a particular location, as opposed to the church universal.

CHURCH, noun. (Theology) The assembly (ekklēsia) of those called out from the world by God through the gospel; in its particular sense, the congregation of believers meeting in a given place, under appointed officers, for worship, instruction, discipline, and fellowship.

2. The local church as the basic unit of Christian community: the New Testament addresses particular congregations, appoints particular elders, exercises particular discipline, and celebrates the ordinances within the bounded fellowship of a specific gathered assembly.

3. Distinct from the universal church (all the elect across all times and places) and the invisible church (the company known only to God): the local church is visible, particular, and covenanted.

Key Scripture

Acts 2:42 — "They were continually devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching, and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread, and to prayer."

Hebrews 10:25 — "not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some — but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day drawing near."

Matthew 18:17 — "And if he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax-gatherer."

1 Timothy 3:15 — "But in case I am delayed, I write so that you will know how one ought to conduct himself in the household of God — which is the church of the living God, the pillar and support of the truth."

Modern Corruption

The online-only “church,” the parachurch substitute for the local assembly, and the “spiritual but not religious” rejection of institutional belonging all represent departures from the apostolic pattern of covenanted, gathered, disciplined local fellowship.

expand to see more

The most common contemporary corruption of the local church is the consumer model: the congregation as a vendor of spiritual goods and services which the individual Christian samples and abandons at will, with no covenant commitment, no accountability, and no discipline. This model reduces the church to a spiritual marketplace and the believer to a customer. It is antithetical to the apostolic pattern. Paul writes to local churches that have specific officers (Phil. 1:1), exercise discipline over specific members (1 Cor. 5), and bear specific mutual obligations (Heb. 10:24–25). The local church is a covenanted body, not a voluntary association that may be left whenever its services displease. Hebrews 10:25’s prohibition of forsaking the assembly was not written for a culture without churches; it was written to people who found excuses—as every generation does—to disengage from the costly bonds of local fellowship.

The digital age has produced a new variant: the “online church” that offers preaching via livestream as a substitute for embodied, covenanted local membership. While online resources may serve those temporarily prevented from gathering, they cannot constitute a church: no ordinances can be administered, no discipline can be exercised, no elders can shepherd, no genuine fellowship can be maintained through a screen. The church is a body (1 Cor. 12), a household (1 Tim. 3:15), a flock (Acts 20:28)—all images requiring physical presence, mutual knowledge, and covenanted accountability. Christianity is an incarnational religion: the Word became flesh (John 1:14), and the church His body must be similarly embodied.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ekklēsia (called-out assembly) and Latin localis (of a place) together name the visible, particular, geographically bounded gathering that is the New Testament’s primary expression of the church.

expand to see more

Greek ekklēsia — assembly, congregation; from ek- (out) + kaleō (to call); names both the universal company of the elect and the particular local gathering that bears the marks of the visible church

Latin locus — place, location; the “local” in “local church” affirms that the church is not an abstraction but a geographically situated, historically particular community

Greek paroikia — sojourn, parish; the word behind “parish”—the local assembly as a community of sojourners gathered in a specific place while awaiting the heavenly city

Hebrew qahal — assembly, congregation; the OT antecedent of ekklēsia—Israel gathered before God at Sinai (Deut. 4:10) prefigures the church assembled before the Lord

Latin congregatio — a gathering together, flock; the root of “congregation,” emphasizing the gathered, visible, particular character of the local assembly

Usage

"The New Testament’s letters are addressed to particular local churches (Corinth, Ephesus, Galatia, Philippi, Colossae, Rome) with specific problems, specific officers, and specific members—evidence that the apostles regarded the local assembly as the normative sphere of Christian life, not an optional supplement to individual faith."

"Church discipline (Matt. 18:15–17) is possible only in a local church: the final appeal is to “the church,” a specific, bounded, accountable assembly whose verdict carries the authority of the keys of the kingdom (Matt. 16:19)."

"The 1689 Baptist Confession locates the fullness of Christ’s kingship in particular churches: “To each of these churches thus gathered, according to His mind declared in His Word, He has given all that power and authority which is any way needful for their carrying on that order in worship and discipline which He has instituted for them to observe” (26.6)."
